(3) The electrons in an atom orbit the nucleus.

B (3) only

The results of the experiment did not give any information on the electrons in an atom.

tb-E202-3.question:
Figure b shows some energy levels of atom P.

If photons having energy of 8.9 eV are incident on a large number of atom P at the first excited state (n = 2), how many spectral lines in the visible region can be obtained subsequently? Given: the energy of a visible light photon ranges from 1.7 eV to 3.2 eV.

A 0

B 1

C 2

D 6
tb-E202-3.reasoning:
The photons can ionize the atoms in state
n = 2. All electron transitions may occur when an ionized atom captures an electron.

However, only the transition from n = 3 to
n = 2 can emit photons within the visible range.

∴ Only 1 spectral line in the visible region can be obtained.

tb-E202-4.question:
An α particle approaches a gold nucleus. Its path is shown in Figure c.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

(1) When the α particle gets closer to the gold nucleus, the force that it experiencs increases.

(2) When the α particle moves along its path, its KE is constant.

(3) The shortest distance between the α particle and the nucleus gives an estimation of the upper limit of the radius of the nucleus.

A (1) only

B (3) only

C (1) and (2) only

D (1) and (3) only
tb-E202-4.reasoning:
When the α particle gets closer to the gold nucleus, its KE is converted into the electric potential energy.

∴ (2) is incorrect.

The α particle is repelled away before colliding with the gold nucleus, so the shortest distance between them must be larger than the radius of the gold nucleus.

∴ (3) is correct.

tb-E202-5.question:
Which of the following statements about the electron in a hydrogen atom is/are correct? It is given that the energy of the electron is –13.6 eV when it is in the ground state.

(1) When the electron is in the ground state, it can escape completely from the nucleus by absorbing a photon of energy 14 eV.

(2) When the electron is in the ground state, it can be excited to the first excited state by absorbing a photon of energy 11 eV.

(3) When the electron drops from an excited state to the ground state, it must emit a photon of energy 13.6 eV.

A (1) only

B (3) only

C (1) and (2) only

D (2) and (3) only
tb-E202-5.reasoning:
E2 − E1 = −13.622 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV

∴ A photon of energy 11 eV cannot excite the electron from the ground state to the first excited state.

∴ (2) is incorrect.

A photon of energy 13.6 eV will be emitted only when an electron drops from n = ∞ to
n = 1.

∴ (3) in incorrect.

(2) The electron in a hydrogen atom can only occupy certain discrete orbits with quantized angular momentum.

(3) When an electron is orbiting in an atom, the electric force between the electron and the nucleus provides the centripetal force.

A (1) only

B (3) only

C (1) and (2) only

D (2) and (3) only
tb-E202-6.reasoning:
According to de Broglie’s explanation, the electron in a hydrogen atom behaves as a stationary wave. The length of its orbit must be an integral multiple of its de Broglie wavelength.

∴ (2) is correct.

tb-E202-10.question:
Which of the following particles may collide inelastically with a hydrogen atom in the first excited state?

(1) An electron of KE 1.6 eV

(2) A proton of KE 2 eV

(3) A neutron of KE 3.5 eV

A (1) only

B (2) only

C (1) and (3) only

D (2) and (3) only
tb-E202-10.reasoning:
The collision is inelastic if the hydrogen atom is raised to a higher energy level.

E∞ − E2 = −E2 = 13.622 = 3.4 eV

E3 − E2 = −13.632 − (−3.4) = 1.89 eV

A neutron of KE 3.5 eV can raise the atom to any higher energy level or even ionize the atom. These collisions are inelastic.

∴ (3) is correct.

A proton of KE 2 eV can raise the atom from the first excited state to the second excited state but an electron of KE 1.6 eV cannot.

∴ (2) is correct but (1) is incorrect.

tb-E202-15.question:
A light ray of power 20 W is shone on a mirror perpendicularly (Fig f ).

Assuming all photons are reflected, what is the magnitude of the average force exerted on the mirror by the photons?

A 0

B 6.67 × 10–8 N

C 1.33 × 10–7 N

D Cannot be determined as the frequency of light is unknown
tb-E202-15.reasoning:

p = Ec

∆p = p − (−p) = 2p = 2Ec

F = ∆pt = 2Ect = 2(20)3.00 × 108 = 1.33 × 10−7 N

tb-E202-21.question:
The result of the Geiger-Marsden experiment gives evidence to the existence of a nucleus in a gold atom (Fig i).

(a) Which type of charge does the nucleus carry? (1 mark)

(b) State the observations in the Geiger-Marsden experiment which lead to the conclusion in

(a). Explain briefly. (3 marks)

(c) (i) How did Rutherford describe the parts in an atom other than the nucleus? (2 marks)

(ii) State two limitations of Rutherford’s atomic model. (2 marks)

(d) State one similarity and one difference between Rutherford’s model and Bohr’s model. (2 marks)
tb-E202-21.answer:
(a) Positive 1A

(b) When a thin gold foil was bombarded with α particles in a vacuum, a very small number of α particles were deflected and a few even bounced back.
1A

This implies that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. 1A

The α particles which happen to come close to the nuclei are repelled by the strong electric force and are therefore deflected or bounce back 1A

(c) (i) Electrons orbit the nucleus along circular paths. 1A

The rest of the atom is largely empty space. 1A

(ii) It cannot explain why atoms are stable. 1A

It cannot explain why atoms of a gas emit EM waves of discrete frequencies only. 1A

(d) Similarity: Electrons orbit the nucleus in circular paths. 1A

Difference: In Rutherford’s model, an electron can occupy any circular path around the nucleus. In Bohr’s model, an electron can only occupy certain discrete orbits. 1A

(Or other reasonable answers.)

tb-E202-22.question:
The light emitted by the Sun passes through the Sun’s atmosphere and produces an absorption spectrum (Fig j).

(a) Explain how the dark lines in the absorption spectrum are formed. (3 marks)

(b) How can the elements in the Sun’s atmosphere be identified by studying these dark lines? (2 marks)

tb-E202-22.answer:
(a) When light of continuous frequency passes through the atmosphere, a photon may be absorbed if it has the exact amount of energy equal to the energy difference between two energy levels. 1A

The electrons raised to higher energy levels would drop back to lower energy levels and re-emit photons in random directions. 1A

Therefore, after the light passes through the atmosphere, the intensity of the light corresponding to the energy values of the absorbed photons decreases significantly. These parts appear as dark lines in the background continuous spectrum. 1A

(b) Each element produces its own characteristic spectral lines. 1A

By matching the frequencies of the dark lines to those produced by each element, 1A

the elements in the Sun’s atmosphere can be identified.

(c) By hf = (13.6 eV)(1b2 − 1a2),

(6.63 × 10−34)(6.89 × 1014)

= (13.6 × 1.60 × 10−19)(122 − 1a2)

1M

a = 5 1A
